VIDEO BEAT: DEEP SPACE WORMHOLES article by Christalene Loren The anomaly appears out of the darkness of space with a pinpoint of fire. It unfolds into a tunnel pulsating with tendrils of light and mystery. At the final frontier lies the wormhole, the enigmatic doorway to the unknown in the popular weekly television series Star Trek: Deep Space Nine. During the summer of 1992, when the pilot for Star Trek: Deep Space Nine was in production, visual effects supervisor Rob Legato made the decision to employ computer animation to create the wormhole effects proposed for the series. Postproduction and visual effects company Rhythm & Hues was commissioned by Paramount Studios to design and create the sequences. The first step was to establish the look. Michael Gibson, a designer-director at Rhythm & Hues, wanted to create an effect that would be visually exciting, as well as ostensibly accurate in terms of current scientific theory. "Since nobody knows what a wormhole looks like," Gibson noted, "or what it would look like to travel through one, I did extensive research both at Cal Tech and wherever I could find books on the subject. I was influenced by the 'Swiss cheese theory' which suggests that space might be shaped in the form of interconnecting points throughout the universe, and that every point is connected to every other point through wormholes that are constantly appearing and disappearing. My emphasis in designing the wormhole was on achieving an organic quality rather than something that looked as if it was a product of mathematical equations. My other priority was to avoid a flat, solid look. I did not want it to appear as if you were falling through a tube with solid walls. In order to achieve these design parameters, we decided to go with a transparent look in multiple layers so that visual information could be seen through the layers, creating a three-dimensional environment." Deep Space Nine, the show's producers turned to For a recurring wormhole effect in Star Trek: Rhythm & Hues for seven basic shots produced digitally using sophisticated particle systems. Armed with black-and-white concept drawings and key-frame airbrush renderings, Gibson and his crew met with executives at Paramount. "One of the advantages of this project was that while both Rob Legato and producer Peter Lauritson had precise ideas regarding the number and types of shots that they wanted, they gave us total artistic freedom in terms of design." Legato and Lauritson needed seven basic shots of the wormhole: three exteriors, three interiors and a separate element that involved a two-second exit from the wormhole as the tunnel opens up and a ship blasts out the other side. To generate the segments, the Rhythm & Hues tech team - consisting of technical director Larry Weinberg, head animator Juck Somsaman, and Mark Henne who provided software support and created the initial cloud animation - employed particle systems on a Silicon Graphics platform, using mostly proprietary software. "After studying Michael's storyboards," said Henne, "the first thing I did in terms of animating the wormhole was to produce animatics which showed the rough timing of the motion. Wire-frame graphics in the form of triangles or squares were used to represent the particles. Adjustments were made in terms of timing and density. Once the animatics were adjusted closer to what Michael intended, we introduced the lighting. At this stage we gave the particles a texture map by painting an image and wrapping it around the geometry of the wire-frame graphics. It's important to remember that while the geometry is moving, the image mapped onto the geometry is also changing in the animation. The geometry becomes invisible and serves as a point of reference for where the texture is located." Once they were able to get a feel for the optimal speed and rotation of the image, the technical team next addressed the problem of eliminating some of the repetition and regularity which tended to diminCINEFEX 55 • 11

ish the desired organic look. "A great deal of work went into this stage," Henne recalled. "The result was an animation of swirling clouds." With approximately forty percent of the work completed, the digital matte elements were delivered to Image G, the company that produces the motion control shots of the Deep Space Nine and the series' spaceships. "From the beginning," Gibson commented, "there was a great deal of interaction between Rhythm & Hues and Image G's director of photography Eric Nash. We had to know what kinds of moves Image G was doing and how their motion control work on the ships was going to link up with the moves we were generating for both the exterior and interior of the wormhole. Our digital matte elements were sent to Paramount where they were transferred to large sheets of Kodalith film. Each sheet of film represented a frame of the animation 12 • CINEFEX 55 sequence for the wormhole exterior. The film was completely black except for the center where the iris of the wormhole opened up. A light was placed behind the sheet of film so that it would shine through the iris of the wormhole and illuminate the model ship placed in front of the film." Meanwhile at Rhythm & Hues, Weinberg continued to work on the exterior views of the wormhole. "To generate the long streams of clouds coming out of its center," Weinberg explained, "Mark Henne modified our 'Bubbles' program so that we were able to link particles flowing out in front with particles that were right behind them. That way, these streams would be spewing out from the center almost like tails from a kite, rather than appearing as separatelyflowing particles." During the next phase of the work, Weinberg added bright particles that swirled around within One of three wormhole interiors designed to be used and reused throughout the series. the clouds, as well as volumetric light emitted from the center of the wormhole along with the spewing particles. Color was determined, also, with an emphasis on purples to suggest the image of a flower opening rather than reds or oranges which might look more like an explosion. "To reinforce the threedimensional illusion," noted Gibson, "Larry and I lit the exterior view as if the source of the light was a sun just off screen in the upper left-hand corner. Lighting the wormhole this way caused the central dome to cast its own shadows across the orbiting rings, creating an impression of volumetric space." In the final stages, Weinberg continued to refine the color, lighting and swirling effects of the animation until all concerned were satisfied. To animate the wormhole's gaseous interior, Juck Somsaman employed an in-house software program called 'Flubber. "The gas core was created out of cylinder shapes modified by the software program to behave like rubber," said Somsaman. "These forms were then texture-mapped, with particle systems applied to create a twinkling effect." Many of the wormhole shots would eventually feature Deep Space Nine shuttlecraft flying through. For these shots, special lighting had to be designed to tie the ships - inside and out - with the luminous wormhole interior. Interactive lighting for the live-action was shot at Paramount Studios under the direction of Rob Legato. "We wrote a number of animation sheets," noted Gibson, "to describe, frame by frame, what was happening to the lighting inside the wormhole so that Image Gand Paramount could reflect that in the interior lighting of their ships." Numerous tests were undertaken to create these animation sheets. The exterior required a particularly novel approach. "We did not have a spaceship database to use for testing the lighting sequences," Weinberg recalled, "so we combined a cow and a biplane database and Juck did a quick rendering of the flying bovine. We shot the aero-cow through the wormhole then to see if the lighting would fall correctly on an object substituted for the Deep Space Nine ships which would be matted in later." "Since the wormhole was designed to be used over and over again in the series," Michael Gibson concluded, "I felt it was important to create enough visual richness and complexity in the imagery so that each time you saw the wormhole and passed through it, you would discover new things. We succeeded in doing that, I think."

QUICK CUTS: UNDER HEAVY CETACEAN article by John Shannon From the giant squid that battled the Nautilus in 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea to the shark that terrorized a small coastal community in Jaws, mechanical marine creatures have inhabited the film world for generations. Rarely, however, has animatronic marine life been featured as prominently as in Warner Brothers' Free Willy. The story revolves around the friendship between a troubled youngster (Jason James Richter) and a killer whale living in captivity in a small marine park in the Pacific Northwest. To play the title role, executive producer Richard Donner and director Simon Wincer had found an orca named Keiko at a marine park in Mexico City. However, when the limitations of working with a real animal became apparent - either because some scenes were too difficult to achieve, or because they might endanger the animal or cast members - the filmmakers turned to Walt Conti to produce a number of mechanical whales that could be used to supplement the real one. No stranger to such undertakings, Conti had worked previously on Star Trek IV, designing and building miniature humpback whales so impressively realistic that many moviegoers left the theater unaware that models had been seen. But Free Willy demanded much more. Because the whale was such an integral part of the story, Conti's goal was to create a character rather than an effect. "It wasn't like the mechanical shark effect in Jaws," Conti noted, "where quick cuts were all that was required. In this instance, the whole second half of the film would be carried by the mechanical whale. So the studio knew they wanted some form of large, free-swimming animatronic." Conti and his crew approached the project by viewing hours of orca footage to analyze such things as speed and range of motion. They also did a variety of motion tests with plywood cutouts. "There are some incredible forces and loads going on inside the Although an actual orca was used for much of Free Willy, a number of scenes employed a fullsize animatronic stand-in built by Walt Conti. real animal to allow it to move gracefully and effortlessly through the water, despite its size and weight," observed Conti. "So in order to build it really strong, while keeping within specific weight requirements, we had to use super-strength steels and aircraft aluminums - really exotic materials." Among the biggest challenges was making the eighteen-foot cinematic cetacean move with lifelike authenticity. The mechanical crew - headed by Greg Richards, Dan Adams, Gene Duval and Scott Riley - faced daunting challenges. "No one had ever successfully built a full-sized, free-swimming animatronic whale before," said Conti. "Just providing enough power and strength to move the flukes through the water required a 150-horsepower motor. And we were constrained by the anatomy of the animal as to where we could put the mechanical works, since everything had to be hidden inside the creature's body." Complicated hydraulics and electrical systems were also designed and built - by John Williams, Jeff Wientraub and Bill Boiko, working under the direction of Ty Boyce - to ensure that the animatronic Willy would move smoothly through the water. "I think the reason animatronic creatures have fallen short in the past is that they moved too slowly or jerkily. Ours contained special circuitry positioned between the operator and the whale; so no matter what the operator did, the movement of the whale was smooth." With all of the actuators and power sources hidden inside the whale, the only external link to a control source was an eight-inch umbilical through which were fed the hydraulic oil and electrical signals. "I had concerns that we would have a problem hiding the umbilical from the camera, but we ended up being able to conceal it very successfully. We could even change its position, placing it on either side or on the bottom, depending on the angle of the shot." The fully animatronic Willy could not only move under its own steam, it was also capable of CINEFEX 55 • 17

reacting to its environment through a wide range of motions that included hydraulically operated head and tail movement, a mouth that opened, pectoral fins that were capable of turning and moving up and down, radio controlled eyes that blinked and moved, and a blow hole that spewed water under pressure based on calculations of a real whale's lung volume. "We went to that degree of detail because it was important for us to replicate the whale's reaction to its environment. It reacts to the boy and it reacts to whatever it sees. It's not just this thing lumbering along." In addition to the mechanical systems, careful attention was given to sculpting the eighteen-foot whale - an exact replica of the real one in Mexico. Supervising the work was Rick Anderson, assisted by Dave Caldwell and Stephanie Englert, with Jonathan Horton sculpting the mouth interior, teeth and tongue. Also tackled was the difficult task of molding and casting the skin - which required three thousand pounds of urethane. "That was a nervous day for us," Conti recalled, "since we had never before poured that much urethane at one time. We had 18 - CINEFEX 55 to do it in twenty minutes and we had to get it right: because after that point, the rubber begins to cure." The true test of the skin came when it was time to submerge the model in water. 'We were concerned about how the skin would look once we got it wet. If it had started to look like wet rubber, it would have obviously destroyed the illusion - but it looked just like a real whale's skin." While the full-scale animatronic was used for a majority of the artificial whale shots -particularly closeups and underwater stunts - a second animatronic was developed specifically for longer shots of surface swimming. Nicknamed 'Turbo Willy, ' the model was an upper-half-only version equipped with a blow hole, two big underwater hydraulic thrusters and dive planes to effect surfacing and diving motions. Again, the concern was to make the swimming moves look as realistic as possible. "I looked at what had been done before," said Conti, "and the problem was that these creatures were too much like submarines. They would just rise and fall on a track; and if the shot went on too long, they looked very stiff." Attached to a three-hundred-foot umbilical and Radio-controlled miniatures were also employed for the capture sequence - photographed by underwater cameraman Pete Romano. maneuvered by a power unit with joysticks located on a nearby barge, the self-contained Turbo Willy could move about freely, and was used extensively during location photography. Along with the two animatronic whales, Conti also created an nonarticulated 'Rubber Willy' for shooting stunts at a distance. "Rubber Willy was really just a full-size dummy. He also served as a backup. In a pinch we could have retrofitted him with actuators since he was built exactly the same as our animatronic Willy. We could have taken the guts out of one and put it in the other. Fortunately, we never had to." Drawing on the technology he had developed for Star Trek IV, Conti also constructed several thirdscale, radio controlled miniatures - in two different sizes to represent adult and baby orcas. "With the big animatronic," noted Conti, "we were always dealing with an umbilical cord, and sometimes that was restrictive. Because the miniatures were totally selfcontained, they were better than the big models for shots where there were multiple whales seen from many angles." The miniatures were used primarily in the film's opening - a capture sequence in which the young Willy is separated from his family. Filmed in an Olympic-size swimming pool dressed to look like the ocean, the sequence required special handling by underwater photographer Pete Romano. "The biggest concern in shooting miniatures is the scale," Romano explained. "You have to compensate for being two feet away from your subject rather than fifteen feet, as would be the case if you were filming a full-size whale. To get as close as possible without sacrificing image clarity, we shot the sequence using a wide-angle lens, and degraded the water considerably with fuller's earth and a combination of other chemicals to make it hazier - just as it would appear if fifteen feet of water separated the camera lens In the end, careful attention to detail and regard for authenticity allayed the filmmakers' initial fears that their main character would be an unaffecting, obviously fake creation. "There had been a lot of apprehension in the beginning," Walt Conti admitted. "Their concern was that they were going to have this big rubber whale flopping around - which would have destroyed the film. But the animatronic worked so well, Jason ended up talking to it and treating it just like the real whale. That was my biggest kick." HYOROILEX

COMPANY FILE: PIXAR article by Estelle Shay With the unveiling of Steven Spielberg's current blockbuster, Jurassic Park, computer generated imaging has taken a quantum leap that may forever change the way effects movies are made. Although an appreciation of CGI and its vast potential has been steadily growing, most people, including many in the effects industry, were wholly unprepared for the astonishing realism of Jurassic Park's digital dinosaurs. Most, but not all. Pixar, the award-winning company responsible for developing the rendering software used by Industrial Light & Magic to create some of Jurassic Park's most memorable images, knew it was simply a matter of time. For more than a decade, the company has been quietly at work creating and refining the tools and systems that helped make the digital breakthrough possible. Organized originally in 1979 as the computer graphics division of Lucasfilm, Pixar's goal was to explore computer imaging technology and project its application to motion picture special effects. Recruited to head the division was Ed Catmull from the New York Institute of Technology's Computer Graphics Laboratory. Taking four of his colleagues from the Institute with him, Catmull proceeded, over the next five years, to assemble a top-notch team of computer experts. Together, they set out to research the relatively new field of computer graphics with the intent of applying whatever findings there might be to the practicalities of film production. Working with their optical brethren at Industrial Light & Magic, the division succeeded in creating brief, but memorable computer graphics sequences for several feature films, including Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan, Return of the Jedi and Young Sherlock Holmes. "Ultimately, the various high technology applications of our work diverged from basic filmmaking," explained Catmull, who still heads the A toy drummer tries to evade a rambunctious toddler in the Oscar-winning animated short, Tin Toy, produced by Pixar, an industry leader in computer animation and software development. management team today, "so in 1986, with the core group still intact, the whole division was spun out as a separate company which became Pixar." The technologies used to accomplish the division's early film successes eventually led to the creation of Pixar's first commercial hardware product - the Pixar Image Computer. In 1990, however, the hardware business was sold in order to allow the team to concentrate exclusively on animation services and software development. Pixar's long-term goal was to produce computer graphics software that was easy to use and economical. "In those early years," observed Catmull, "there were industry attempts to do computer animation, but the economics never made any sense. So our goal - even back at Lucasfilm - was to develop rendering technology in preparation for the time when the costs would be right. When we founded the company, they still weren't right. But we continued our research and development by consciously doing a film every year in an effort to improve the tools and to get a better handle on production." Over the years, Pixar's persistence paid off. In 1988, the company introduced a 3-D rendering software product, known as RenderMan, which revolutionized computer imaging and recently won recognition by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences for its contribution to computer animation and 3-D computer effects. A series of short computer animated films, produced internally to showcase their capabilities while honing their skills, has won every major award available to animated films, including an Academy Award nomination for Luxo, Jr. andan Academy Award for Tin Toy — the first ever bestowed on a completely computer animated subject. QUICK CUTS: ONCE MORE INTO THE ABYSS article by David C. Fein Pressured by exhibitors to keep running times in the two-hour range, a growing number of filmmakers have turned to home video - specifically the laserdisc format - as a means of presenting more complete versions of their films. Others are seeking even grander alternatives. For his 'special edition' laserdisc release of Aliens, director James Cameron inserted seventeen minutes of previously excised footage that expanded upon his vision and won renewed admiration and revenue for his already megahit film. The success of this endeavor prompted Cameron to approach Twentieth Century Fox regarding a similarly expanded version of The Abyss, which during postproduction had been shorn of a major subplot involving escalating tensions among the world's superpowers and a gigantic tidal wave orchestrated by nonterrestrials as a warning to mankind. The difference was that Cameron wanted the restoration completed on film - Aliens had been done on video - to allow for a possible theatrical reissue similar to the one that had prompted critical reevaluation of Blade Runner. Fox agreed to finance the endeavor, which entailed not only the insertion of twenty-eight minutes of previously unseen production footage, but also a major soundtrack reconstruction since the original production audio had been unaccountably lost. The tidal wave sequence - produced by Industrial Light & Magic, which had also contributed the pseudopod water probe - begins in the underwater cityship where the alien NTIs communicate with Bud Brigman (Ed Harris) by projecting newsreel footage of warfare and human atrocities onto a wall of water. To accomplish the illusion, rear-projected video footage was directed through water to give it a fluidlike 'ruffle, then reflected onto a wall screen placed at the edge of the set. Another rear projection, this one used to create the illusion that the set continued off into the liquid expanse, was reflected next to the moving footage to complete the illusion that the surface was indeed water. As a live newscast flashes before him, Bud observes a television reporter on the beach in Santa Monica covering an awesome two-thousand-foot-tall tidal wave which has appeared out of nowhere and is advancing inexorably toward the shore. Subsequent scenes - representing similar occurrences worldwide - were then shown more clearly as the film's point of view shifts from the NTI ark to the actual locations being threatened. With the exception of one shot that was to be generated from scratch, visual effects supervisor Dennis Muren and his ILM team returned to the original film elements they had created four years earlier. "I knew there was a chance of this happening a long " observed Muren. "Jim had said that we time ago,' might finish these shots someday and release the movie the way it was meant to be. So we weren't that surprised when we heard he was doing it." With only limited time and funding to complete their earlier work, Muren and company had to improvise in finishing two of the Santa Monica shots. Both contained elements from the location shoot that were discolored in sections where they overlapped the inserted tidal wave. It was decided early on that the best solution was to employ computer technology. "We couldn't afford to recomposite the shots, so we took temp composites and image-processed the hell out of them over a period of about three weeks. We began about three composites away from the final and managed to get the shots pretty close to the way we wanted by working digitally instead of optically, painting in areas to get the color and lighting balances to come together in a realistic and natural way. A lot of the work involved correcting the densities of the dark trees. Luckily there was enough information in the shots to allow us to lighten them up digitally." For shots of the wave advancing and receding, actual big-wave footage shot in Hawaii was enlarged and matted in to deliver the most realistic image. However, since no wave in history has ever slowed and stood frozen for a camera, it was necessary to create one that would. Originally the crucial stopping shot was to have consisted of real wave footage reduced in speed and then morphed to create smooth intermediate frames. However, since technology had evolved greatly in the past four years, it was decided that a more dynamic effect could be created wholly within the digital realm. "Our skill level had improved dramatically since The Abyss," commented Muren. "We had spent a little time back then trying to create the wave with computers, but found that our tools and our skill level at the time were such that we just couldn't get it done in the necessary time frame. It was very complicated and our tests weren't really that encouraging." Reconceptualizing the shot, Cameron drew a new storyboard giving the wave greater depth and a stronger crest than it had in the original. Then, working from a model rendered in the computer, the ILM computer graphics team began to create surface texture for the wave. "The surface is not photographic images scanned in and texture-mapped onto the wave, as you might expect. Everything on the surface was a calculated design. You can get a lot more precision that way and a lot more exacting detail than you can get with the texture maps, as long as your parameters are precise." The sky above the wave was the only portion of the shot taken directly from a photographic element. It was also used as a source of color and light reflecting onto the wave. "There was a tremendous amount of skill involved in modeling the wave and running the RenderMan shaders to get the surface detail to appear like water. Joe Letteri worked on it for five weeks and was responsible for much of the look. Four years more experience, and a lot more computer horsepower, made all the difference in what we could do." A closer view of the Santa Monica wave had been completed during the original postproduction phase and was incorporated unaltered into the special edition. Against a wall of standing water - produced simply by shooting directly down onto San Francisco Bay from the Golden Gate Bridge - were composited a miniature flying helicopter and scores of circling seagulls photographed at a local garbage dump. Foreground extras were shot on a bluescreen stage in groups that were then matted into the background at different locations and distances to impart a suitable sense of scale and depth. Other effects completed during the original production included shots of the wave rising and being held suspended near the Statue of Liberty in New York, over the Golden Gate Bridge and the streets of San Francisco, and at a Soviet naval installation on the Kamchatka Peninsula. The Huston model - about twenty feet long by three feet tall - was built over a motion control mechanism and had a drum underneath it to create a sense of its rolling forward in a wavelike manner. An optical lens flare was the final sweetening element. With the twelve-month restoration complete, Cameron and his co-workers were at last able to see The Abyss as it was originally scripted and shot. QUICK CUTS: HAIL TO THE IMPOSTOK article by Bob Peishel Given the climate of political disenchantment that has persisted through severai administrations, the time was more than ripe for Warner Brothers' recent release of its comedy Dave, directed by Ivan Reitman. Taking aim at Washington politics, Dave is the story of presidential look-alike and all-around good guy, Dave hovic, who is recruited to impersonate President Bill Mitchell during a brief public appearance, but ends up extending the charade and winning the hearts of the populace. Buena Vista Visual Effects was brought in to create the film's visual illusions, which included fifteen shots utilizing extensive matte paintings, as well as a complex traveling split-screen shot in which Kovic and Mitchell - both played by Kevin Kline - appear simultaneously. The split-screen shot occurs when Dave and the president meet face-to-face for the first and only time. "It was Ivan Reitman's contention that if we sold it really well once, we didn't need to do it again," recalled Harrison Ellenshaw, visual effects supervisor for Dave and head of BVVE. The shot, which begins from an angle over Dave's shoulder as Mitchell enters the room, then dollies around to the side as the president walks toward Dave - revealing both characters in the same frame - required the use of BVVE's real-time motion control system to create identical camera moves on both sides of the split. "It worked out well because our real-time motion control rig is designed to run on a curved track," explained Ellenshaw, "and a curved track was required for the camera move Ivan needed." Logistically, the scene was complicated by the fact that filming was to take place in an actual hotel room - the presidential suite at the Biltmore Hotel in Los Angeles. Consequently, the effects team could have access to the location for setting up only on the morning of the shoot. To prepare for the shot, Ellenshaw and effects Buena Vista Visual Effects produced an elaborate motion control split-screen shot to establish actor Kevin Kline in his dual role in Dave. consultant Peter Montgomery visited the Biltmore to measure and diagram the suite in great detail. Armed with this information, the Buena Vista Visual Effects crew replicated the room and hallway on their own stage so that the move with the real-time motion control rig could be worked out and programmed in advance. On the day of the shoot, the rig was set up with the predetermined moves in computer memory. "As luck would have it, Ivan decided that the move needed to be changed," Ellenshaw recalled, "so Peter and the motion control operator, Les Bernstien, literally had to program a new move right then. The beauty of our real-time motion control rig is that that's no big problem. The first unit camera operator - in this case, Bill Roe - can operate pan and tilt by means of remote wheels, just like a 'real' camera." Once the new move was selected and refined, the 'A' half of the scene was filmed. This covered Kline's entrance, as Mitchell, and the background portion of the scene when first viewed from behind Dave. It also included Secret Service agent Duane Stevensen (Ving Rhames), whom Reitman wanted in the shot. The move was especially tricky because of the backpan involved. As Montgomery and Bernstien filmed the plate, they not only had to keep the move as smooth as possible, but as the camera came around, they also needed to ensure that both characters, when composited, would stay properly framed in the shot. When Reitman was satisfied with both the move and Kline's timing, the 'B' side of the shot was set up. For this side - which had Dave in the foreground - a rear-light bluescreen was erected and placed back in the doorway, opposite the actor. Although it would have been simpler to pull the bluescreen forward into the set, reducing the amount of roto work involved in compositing the shot, its position in the doorway allowed for the rear lights to be placed in the hall. Great care was taken to keep the lighting identical to the 'A' half of the shot. Upon completion of the setup and filming of the CINEFEX 55 • 35

'B' side, the effects crew employed a video effects unit from Video Assist Systems to produce a rough moving split on the spot. "This was very helpful," Ellenshaw noted, "because we could see which takes worked best and put them together right on the set. It also got people very excited about how well the shot was working." Because of the complexity of the split-screen shot and its importance to the film, Reitman requested that it be given priority and delivered quickly. In order to meet the deadline, the BVVE team selected Composite Image Systems - Hollywood - with whom they had worked on several shots for Honey, I Blew Up the Kid - to assemble the shot rather than wait for their own digital film system which was just being installed. At CIS, the film-to-digital transfer was done at high resolution. Then, articulate rotoscope and moving split work was accomplished before compositing the shot, also at high resolution to give the entire effect a seamless film look. Digital paint effects were handled by Danny Mudgett and 36 * CINEFEX 55 digital compositing was by Peter Koczera and Price Pethel. The digital master was then recorded back to film at more than 2000 lines of resolution using the company's EFILM process. Ellenshaw credited Kline with helping to pull off the full effect. "Obviously the reveal is very tricky - the fact that you dolly past one character to see the other one coming in. But if you study the shot carefully, Kevin is doing a remarkable job of looking at himself off both sides and interacting with his twin. Keep in mind he had to react to thin air. It must be difficult to focus on nothing - but he really pulled it off. And that's what sells the shot." Every bit as challenging were the thirteen matte paintings of the White House and city surroundings used in conjunction with partial sets created to represent the White House south lawn and the portico entrance. "The only real shots of the White House are those taken from across the street or from the roof of an adjacent building," noted matte painting supervisor Paul Lasaine. "The matte paintings of the White Since access to the White House was limited matte paintings by Paul Lasaine were used to broaden the scope of partial set pieces. House were used in scenes where the script called for action such as the helicopter landing on the White House lawn or where someone was required to drive through the gates toward the entrance." One particularly effective painting featured a night view of Washington D.C. as a backdrop to a hillside picnic scene where Dave finally befriends First Lady Ellen Mitchell (Sigourney Weaver) after she discovers the ruse. "This shot needed to be both romantic and real," explained effects producer Lynda Lemon. "Creating the proper mood involved adding some twinkling city lights, a blinking aircraft warning light, and street traffic simulated through the use of a moire pattern." Another complicated shot requiring a combination of matte paintings and split-screens was a critical scene in the House of Representatives chambers where President Dave feigns a stroke. Unable to obtain permission to shoot in the real location, Reitman staged the scene at the State Capitol building in Richmond, Virginia, which had only four rows of seating. In order to duplicate the House chambers, a matte painting depicting additional rows was used in combination with five or six split-screens involving live-action shots of congressmen clapping, then standing and rushing forward as Dave collapses. "Those were pretty wild shots," recalled Lasaine. "We would grab the last two or three rows in a section, and then matte cameraman Wally Schaab would reposition that piece, changing the framing and offsetting the timing so it didn't look like we had the same people all doing the same thing. For the scene where the congressmen all rushed forward, passing in front of each other, hours and hours of articulate rotoscoping were required." Since Buena Vista Visual Effects was still getting its digital system on line, all of the elements in the shot were composited conventionally on a Mechanical Concepts optical printer. "A movie like this," concluded Lasaine, "is the classic effects film - because if you do your job right, nobody even knows you exist. One of our animators recently related a conversation he had with a fellow animator at another effects house. His friend said, 'I don't like matte paintings because, first of all, I've never seen one that works.' Our guy asked, 'Well, what did you think of the matte paintings in Dave?' And his friend replied, 'What matte paintings?' We considered that the ultimate compliment." DAVE HL 2 / TB

Youngsters who approach the school field trip to the natural history museum with little more than apathy come excitedly to life in the presence of the dinosaur skeletal exhibits. For many of us, that enthusiasm never fades, even with the advent of adulthood. We remain delighted by the dinosaurs' size and majesty, bewildered by their unexplained disappearance, humbled by their te nacious endurance on a planet that, in geological time, we have only just begun to occupy. Paleontology was the science that arose out of this fascination. Over the course of nearly two hundred years, scientists have painstakingly uncovered the fossilized clues that have solved some of the mysteries surrounding the prehistoric creatures. Their efforts, though laudable, have been frustratingly insufficient for the avid dinosaur fan, however. No matter how carefully reconstructed the skeleton, no matter how brilliantly rendered the illustration, no matter how scientifically sound the theory, paleontology has never been able to provide the dinosaur enthusiast with what he wants most - to see the living creatures for himself. That wish fulfillment has been the province of the movies. From the silent The Lost Worldto the masterful King Kong, from the popular One Million Years B.C. to the ambitious When Dinosaurs Ruled the Earth, filmmakers have - with a greater or lesser degree of skill and authenticity - attempted to meet our heartfelt desire to know the beasts. This summer, that cinematic tradition has been brought to fruition with the release of the ultimate dinosaur movie - Jurassic Park - a master stroke of filmmaking made possible by some of the most innovative and astonishing effects ever put to film. In a serendipitous bit of timing, Jurassic Park began production just as dinosaurs were enjoying a resurgence of popularity. This groundswell of interest in things prehistoric, coupled with the fact that Jurassic Park was to be directed by Steven Spielberg, suggested that the movie had the potential to be a major cinematic event. And it was. In the weeks leading up to its June release, Jurassic Park became the hot topic of conversation, as well as the subject of countless news and entertainment programs. Newspapers ran ads that featured a daily countdown to the premiere. Dinosaur documentaries, both new and old, appeared on television. McDonald's 'dino-sized' their foodstuff; cuddly T-rex's and brachiosaurs filled toy stores; and, when opening day finally arrived, lines of moviegoers wrapped around theaters foretold of the record-breaking $50 million debut weekend Jurassic Park would enjoy. The phenomenon began as a best-selling novel by Michael Crichton, an author and filmmaker with a distinctive style that skillfully blended thrilling fiction and hard science in books such as The Andromeda Strain and Congo, and in films such as Westworld and Coma. With Jurassic Park, published in 1990, Crichton returned to a theme he had explored repeatedly in his work - the dire consequences of human interference with natural law. The novel is set on Isla Nublar, an island off the coast of Costa Rica where fifteen dinosaur species have been successfully cloned by a team of genetic engineers hired by megalomaniac John Hammond. Hammond's dream is to create the ultimate theme park - Jurassic Park - and, after five years of top-secret development, it is nearing completion. To satisfy anxious investors, Hammond invites a small team of scientists to inspect the soon-to-be-opened facility and give it their stamp of approval. Among the luminaries are paleontologists Alan Grant and Ellie Sattler, and mathematician lan Malcolm. Also along for the excursion are attorney Donald Gennaro - there to represent the investors - and Hammond's visiting grandchildren, Tim and Alexis Murphy. After the group embarks on the tour, a computer shutdown deactivates the electrified fences that surround each dinosaur paddock and, within hours, chaos of the prehistoric kind is unleashed upon the park. So promising was the novel as a film vehicle that a furious bidding war involving several major studios and some top Hollywood directors erupted before the book was even published. Among the first to indicate interest in the property, Steven Spielberg and his Amblin Entertainment ultimately emerged victorious. Indeed, the story was ideally suited to the sensibilities the director had revealed in his previous films. It had the managainst-nature suspense of Jaws; the elements of wonder and awe evident in both Close Encounters and E.T.; and the fastpaced action of the Indiana Jones trilogy. A better marriage of material and director was hard to imagine. Yet the project was so complex, so fraught with seemingly insurmountable challenges, that three full years would elapse before Jurassic Park was finally revealed to moviegoers. From the outset, Spielberg had maintained that he wanted to achieve a large percentage of his dinosaur shots with full-size, mechanical creatures. In fact, his initial impulse had been to explore the feasibility of a freestanding robotic tyrannosaur that could actually walk. As disappointing as the mechanical ape in the King Kong remake had been, as harrowing as the director's own experience with a mechanical shark on Jaws, Spielberg still harbored the optimistic hope that advancements in robotics since those earlier films would provide him with viable characters he could shoot on stage, in real time, without having to rely too much on visual effects. Lantieri was in on Spielberg's early exploration of full-scale robotics. "We looked at the 'King Kong' attraction in Florida, which Steven really liked. We also looked at Dinamation International, which is a company that does dinosaur exhibits. We talked to the Henson organization, which was doing Dinosaurs for television." The most serious discussions involved Bob Gurr, the designer of the 'King Kong' attraction. "Gurr is a key player in the design of creatures for amusement parks, and he thought his company might be able to build a robotic T-rex that could actually walk around. Their plan was to build something with motion sensors that was completely balanced, so that as it started to take a step, it would sense the center of gravity going over and adjust its balance with its tail. It would have been an extremely high-tech kind of thing." In spite of high hopes, it became evident before long that a walking T-rex was not a viable option. "We contacted NASA." Lantieri said, "Cornell University, MIT, Cal Tech - people who are doing research on developing walking critters on Mars and the moon - and we found out what it took for them to get something that would take even one step, the kind of feedback and balance that was necessary. Everyone agreed that a freestanding T-rex that would plug in and walk from one stage to the other might be too high an expectation." Though disappointed, Spielberg, too, realized the impracticality of the robotic approach. "What they had with the 'King Kong' attraction at Universal was basically lightweight inflatable balloons with fur on them," Spielberg noted. "But our animals had to have marbled, textured skin that could stretch and muscles that could bulge. So we abandoned the idea of full-size robotics - although I still wanted full-size dinosaurs." The job of creating those full-scale dinosaurs - mechanized through more traditional movie means such as cable and radio controls - landed heavily into the lap of Stan Winston, creator of animatronic characters such as the alien queen in Aliens and the endoskeletons in both Terminator films. Working in close collaboration with Winston, Lantieri was tasked with devising the various support structures necessitated by the enormous size of the full-scale creations. "Stan handled anything that was skinned with rubber," said Lantieri, "while I tackled anything that was used to support and interface with his dinosaurs. It was a tremendous job - way beyond the standard mechanical effects you see in a normal show." To deal with the massive assignment, Lantieri divided his team into two groups - one to deal with straightforward effects such as producing rain and providing rigs for stage effects, and another to work directly with Winston on more unusual dinosaur rigs. "My 'dino-interface' team had to find out what support systems might be necessary and then invent those things," Lantieri explained. "At this point, we were really just guessing: 'Okay, this dinosaur is going to weigh this much - how are we going to move it?' 'You build the thing from the neck up and we'll build everything from the neck down.' 'We'll figure out how to move it up, pan, tilt and hold all the weight if you can do the finer moves and keep all the skin looking great.' There was nowhere to call to find out how to do this kind of stuff. It was just a matter of putting our heads together." Like Lantieri, Stan Winston had been a part of the Jurassic Park project even before Universal had given the film the goahead, engaging key illustrator Mark 'Crash' McCreery to produce a series of detailed dinosaur sketches to help keep Universal interested in the project. "There were constant rumors that Jurassic Park was never going to get made," Winston recalled, "but we just kept plodding forward with these sketches. Initially, Crash did some very exciting sketches of the T-rex, which I think helped to keep the excitement going for the movie. And in the beginning, these sketches were on me - I wasn't being paid by either Universal or Amblin. They were just something to show my good faith and interest in the project." "We were working on Terminator 2," McCreery elaborated, "and Stan pulled me off of that project and had me start drawing a T-rex, which was a major character in the book. I'd been trying to keep up on all of the current information, all the new findings; and I incorporated much of what I knew into the first drawing, which was a running T-rex. It took me a couple of weeks to draw that one. At that stage I was just having fun with it. Then I did a second drawing which showed a T-rex in a jungle scene. There weren't any models to go by for these things, so it was a matter of working it out in my head and on the drawing board." Winston showed McCreery's initial two drawings to Spielberg, who came back with design suggestions of his own. "Spielberg thought the feet on my original drawings were a little too birdlike and small; he thought it should have larger legs to hold the weight of it. He also thought the forearms were a little weak. Stan and I spent months redesigning this thing over and over again." McCreery also began drawing the other dinosaurs that

were slated to be in the film. "I drew raptors, the dilophosaur, both a fully grown and a baby triceratops, a brachiosaur and a gallimimus. This was still early on - we didn't even know if we had the film yet. It was a real secret project. Stan just kept me locked up in this little room and he would slide food under the door from time to time." Even in these earliest drawings, Winston and company - dinosaur fanatics, one and all - were committed to rendering the creatures with as much scientific authenticity as possible. "The only creative liberties we took with the dinosaurs were in areas where there would have been guesswork involved anyway," Winston asserted. "There were no hardcore facts to tell us exactly what the skin texture was or exactly what the coloring was in these animals. It was just a guess based on bone structure and what we knew about existing animals. Even paleontologists depend a great deal on current, similar animals to figure out what dinosaurs might have looked like. We did the same thing, looking at nature and making our best estimations." Visually incorporated into the designs was the fairly recent scientific hypothesis suggesting that dinosaurs, rather than disappearing from the earth in some cataclysmic manner, merely evolved into modern-day birds. "I made the bird connection very obvious in my designs," stated McCreery. "On the T-rex, I made the feet look like eagle talons. The raptor's eyes were very birdlike as well. Even the spitter was somewhat chicken-like - hopping and chirping and things like that. All of the dinosaurs were kind of a melding of bird and lizard." Another important consideration in the design process was making the dinosaurs look like animals rather than monsters - a directive that had come from Spielberg himself. "I wouldn't let anyone call them monsters or creatures," Spielberg said. "We called them animals, or dinosaurs, or by their names. We were really strict about that, because we thought it was important. These animals may be able to kill you, but it is not their primary function in life." The Winston team agreed wholeheartedly with Spielberg's naturalistic philosophy. "The way monsters are depicted in films," said McCreery, "they are always mean, always pissed off, always after something. But the dinosaurs in Jurassic Park, with the exception of the raptors, aren't pissed off all the time. They are animals and they act like animals. Both the spitter and the T-rex have a certain curiosity about them in the movie: the raptors have a premeditated intelligence about them; the brachiosaur comes to graze at a tree and the characters feed it. In King Kong, that same dinosaur knocks a raft over and chews a guy up and spits him out - that's a monster. In Jurassic Park, we felt the dinosaurs deserved not to be thought of as terrorizing monsters, but as actual, living animals that once existed on earth." With the maquettes completed and approved, the Winston art department next had to devise a means to replicate them in full scale - an unusually difficult task because of the size of the dinosaurs. "The first part of our job was artistic," Winston commented, "which was no problem. The artists here are unsurpassed when it comes to sketching and drawing and sculpting. But the second part of the job was technical - how were we going to sculpt things that were this big? With the T-rex, for example, how were we going to enlarge our fifth-scale sculpture five times and make it look as good at eighteen feet tall as it did in miniature? Everyone was worried about it because we'd never done anything like this before." The problem of how to expand the models up to full size was solved by slicing the rigid foam maquettes into precise crosssections, as if slicing a loaf of bread. Using an opaque projector, the Winston crew then projected each slice at five times its original size onto plywood, drawing the outline and allowing two inches all the way around for a thickness of clay. Each plywood piece was numbered, cut out and then reassembled, creating a basic sculpting form around which the artists could apply clay. "All the plywood pieces were put numerically back in order and then hooked to an armature, Mahan explained. "That gave us the entire length and a fair amount of proportion right there. We sculpted over that." The largest of the full-scale sculptures were the tyrannosaurus rex and the triceratops. Fortunately, since the script called for a sick triceratops that was only to be seen lying on its side, the animal could be sculpted in a prone position, alleviating support problems inherent in a sculpture of its size. "The DID armature had encoders at all the pivot points. Animators could position it, and each position would be recorded in the computer through software developed by Brian Knep. They could also do a quick shade to see a solid version of it. In that way, it was miles ahead of stop-motion animation. With stop-motion, you may bring a video camera along so you can look at what you have done; but if there's a mistake, there's no hope of going back and fixing it." "We knew this would be the first time that most of the people at Tippett's place would be using computers," noted Brian Knep, "so we had to provide a simple, bomb-proof interface. The hope was that they would be able to just turn on the computer, run the program, do their animation and send the resulting files to us at ILM to render. At the same time, however, we didn't know what problems we would run into; so we had to write code that was versatile and easy to change." With supervisor of software and digital technology Thomas A. Though most of the Jurassic Park stage work was accomplished at Universal, the T-rex attack was photographed on Stage 16 at Warner Brothers, one of the biggest soundstages in Hollywood. Throughout the preparation phase, no sequence had been more problematic than the T-rex attack on the main road. Facing the filmmakers was the challenge of how to create a twentyfoot-tall predatory dinosaur that could perform complex actions such as tearing down a fence and ripping into tour vehicles, and interact closely with the human characters. Initially, the production had determined that some sort of miniature puppet would be augmented with full-size insert props - an approach that had served creature films routinely for decades. "There was to be a full-size insert head," explained Winston, "a full-size tail, full-size feet, et cetera. It was a budgetary decision at the time, just to create what he had to have for the T-rex full-size. At one point, there was also going to be a full-size sleeping body. It was just going to be lying there, so there wasn't any concern about whether it would work or not - but it would have still been an enormous job, sculpturally, just because of its size. We also discussed making a fifth-scale T-rex rod puppet. The problem there was that we would have had to design fifth-scale sets - and we would still have to shoot it bluescreen, so what would be the point? I liked the idea of using a variety of sizes for each animal; but again, we were limited to a certain extent by the budget. We simply did not have the resources to build every element we thought we could possibly use." At that early stage, Winston proposed to Amblin that the sleeping T-rex be created in miniature. "I asked if we could take the money that would be saved there and put it into connecting the full-size head and body and tail and feet - thereby allowing me to sculpt the entire T-rex and then break it mechanically at the belly so we could see most of the animal full-size. I thought it would be very limiting for Steven to try and get a shot of the head without seeing the rest of the body. But with the full body connected, it would be very easy for him to frame out the legs. So I expressed my wish to sculpt the entire T-rex and then, from that, build a full-size animatronic version from the belly up." Cutting the sleeping T-rex altogether, Spielberg approved the plan and Winston began developing the full-scale mechanical T-rex - a process that would evolve over the next two years. In selling the concept of a full-size animatronic rig, Winston had committed himself to an unprecedented enterprise. Enormous mechanical props had certainly been attempted before, but usually with results ranging from disappointing to disastrous. The amusement park industry had fared better with their robotic creations, but those successes had been achieved in part because of the generally static nature of the attractions. "Amusement park creatures of this size move slowly," Winston commented, "and their range of motion is next to nowhere. Typically with something like this, you are told the move the thing needs to make, and you say, 'Fine, I'll go program it in the computer and we'll have it for you in a few weeks.' And then, that is all it will do - that one movement over and over and over again. But the T-rex had to be able to act, in real time, right there on the set, just like any other actor. "Another problem we were looking at was how to get the skin to move realistically on something this big. We had built a fourteen-foot queen alien for Aliens, but that was an exoskeleton - there was no skin, no organic exterior problems to deal with. Here, we were contemplating a T-rex that needed to turn its head and stretch its neck in all directions - and to do that, we were talking about skin having to stretch a distance of feet, not inches. What kind of material would do that? How were we going to keep it from looking floppy or folding in the wrong places? What about the 'waga waga' factor? Anything that big, moved with speed, will have a certain vibrating movement when it comes to a stop. How were we going to eliminate that? These were just some of the problems we were faced with when we started this - and they were enormous." The difficult task had begun with the sculpting of the T-rex which, when completed, stood more than twenty feet tall and extended forty feet from nose to tail. Next came the molding process. "Years ago," noted John Rosengrant, "the T-rex probably would have been made out of a huge stone mold with a big framework on it - we had heard of big molds being made that way, and we dreaded the idea. Instead, we broke it down into nine mold pieces for the head-to-tail section, another six pieces per leg, and two molds for each of the arms. In the past, a dividing wall on the piece to create the mold was always laid up in clay or with metal shims that were stuck down into the sculpture - which sometimes destroyed it or made for an edge that was not very clean. So on the T-rex we made foamcore patterns and cut those out and propped them up with little thin sticks that went into the sculpture, but left only a toothpick-size hole." From the molds, foam latex skins were produced and painted

The size and weight of the T-rex would require advanced hydraulics systems - an unexplored territory for Winston and his team. Aware of the complexity of the technical challenge ahead of him, Winston hired hydraulics engineer Craig Barr to consult with the studio in their development of the T-rex. "I hired Craig on a trial basis and we ended up going on field trips together, visiting robotics factories to get some ideas of different hydraulics. He became an essential part of this project." With a background as a producer for Universal Studios' King Kong' and 'Jaws' attractions, Barr was well acquainted with the problems and complications inherent in large-scale robotics. "I kept telling Stan: 'This is big, bad stuff! This is equipment that can hurt people, and it can't be fixed on the fly. There has to be a lot of preplanning." Barr's first assignment was to bring Winston's first-rate mechanical team - Evan Brainard, Charles Lutkus and Richard Landon - up to speed in the unfamiliar arena of large-scale hydraulics. "Everyone was very eager to learn. As fast as I could dish it out, they were gobbling it up and spitting it right back out." Barr was also key to signing on experienced hydraulics engineers. "I brought in Lloyd Ball, a hydraulic engineer who works in the industry. I also got Tim Nordella on the project, one of the lead designers on the 'E.T.' attraction. I found help in the aerospace industry for things like making sure we had the proper valve sizes so the figure would be strong enough. I brought in Steve MacIntyre from Anitech, a company that builds animation control systems." With the hydraulics team assembled, Barr and the Winston mechanical crew began the slow and laborious process of designing the hydraulic systems which would drive every function of the T-rex, with the exception of its radio controlled eyes. "I would take a broomstick and move it, and ask, 'Is this how fast you want the arm to move?' We would measure that and write down X inches per second. We went through each move that way." "To solve the problem," said Barr, "we came up with an electronic circuit that we injected into the standard position servo loop. Every channel had a servo card that we could tune so that it would have certain ramps, certain accelerations, certain characteristics. We went a step further and added accelerometers. There were two separate loops, and we fed information back to the position loop that would actually cancel the vibration. It was a real-time feedback system, always out there looking for certain accelerations. We could say, 'Okay, if you ever see it doing this, go ahead and send this signal back to the servo card.' So if the rig was shaking in one direction, the system would bias it the other way and just cancel that shake out." We literally created the biggest effects in motion picture history - and we did something historic in that we presented the dinosaurs more authentically than anyone ever has before." Phil Tippett and his company created dinosaurs, and in so doing merged moviemaking history with its future. "The significance of this whole endeavor," Tippett asserted, "was not only to make the dinosaurs as living, viable things, but to help the traditional craft and craftspeople, to help stop-motion animators get into the world of the computer. In the beginning, the decision to go with computer animation was a devastating one for me, but it turned out to be a good thing. The motion picture industry now has a new tool, and that new tool can be expanded into a multiplicity of different applications. It annoys me to see recent articles about the extinction of stop-motion, as if the only way to sell the new tool is to denigrate the past and say that the historical track that was taken is now worthless and has no meaning. That is simply not true. The impact of Jurassic Park on stop-motion is that there was a tremendous reassessment of the approach. If it is true there has been extinction, it is also true that a phoenix has risen from the ashes." Dennis Muren and Industrial Light & Magic also created dinosaurs, and in so doing completed a learning curve that began seven years ago with the water pseudopod in The Abyss. "We called what we did in Jurassic Park 'full-motion' animation," said Muren. "In this case, it just happened to be full-motion dinosaurs. But it would not have to be dinosaurs - it could be aliens or phantoms or ghosts or dogs. I'm hoping filmmakers will be able to extrapolate, that they'll be able to see the potential for creating characters. What we had in this movie were dinosaurs with an attitude. Once you get that attitude across, then you have a performance. And if you have a performance, you have an actor, whether it's a person or a dog or whatever. Writers and directors don't have to worry anymore about how to get their ideas on the screen. Computer graphics can do it." For Steven Spielberg, a lover of old movies and old moviemaking techniques, there was a tinge of regret mixed with the excitement over the technological achievements of Jurassic Park and what they might mean to the future of filmmaking. "There is something to be said for the pure art of manipulating a wire and latex model," Spielberg reflected. "And so, even as CG becomes more affordable and is used more often, I hope stop-motion will still be around as an art form for enthusiasts and students of film to enjoy. I hope artists will still have their hands in the pipe cleaners and wires and armatures and clay, and will continue to create. With CG, we are essentially taking the paintbrush away from Matisse and giving him a keyboard. I don't think Matisse would have appreciated that." COMMERCIAL SPOT: EVOLUTIONARY AUTO article by Jody Duncan The longing for speed and adventure that burns within the heart of nearly every potential car buyer was very effectively tapped by the Ketchum Advertising Agency in a spot for Acura that indelibly linked their client's product to the excitement and highperformance qualities of a racing car. In 'Evolution,' a real Formula One racecar enters frame and then, in transformer-like fashion, mechanically evolves into an Integra three-door hatchback. The low-key and elegantly simple commercial ends with the Integra driving out of frame, leaving viewers with the impression that the entire transformation has been effected before their eyes. Entrusted with the execution of the spot were director Steve Beck and a visual effects crew at Industrial Light & Magic headed by supervisor Rick Schulze and special effects keys Joe Fulmer and Dave Heron. Knowing only that they wanted the racecar to evolve into the Integra, but uncertain as to the particulars of how the transformation should take place, Ketchum gave the effects team creative leeway in devising the specific style for the metamorphosis. "ILM was very involved in developing the look of the spot," commented effects producer Clint Goldman. "There had been a lot of automobile morph commercials, and Ketchum knew they wanted something different. Steve came up with the idea of a transformer-type effect - kind of like a James Bond gag - and they liked that. The goal was to create something that would appear to happen in front of the camera in one take." The effects team first produced a series of drawings and a variety of small transformer-type toys to determine how the effect could be achieved in full scale. "We built a little model of the Integra and another little model of the Formula One," said Goldman, "just so we could move the pieces around and experiment. We determined from those models that we shouldn't move all the separate sections of the Stagehands at Industrial Light & Magic prepare a Formula One racecar for a commercial in which it transforms mechanically into an Acura Integra. car, because that would be too much to see; but we couldn't show too little either, because then it wouldn't be interesting enough. So we had to come up with what pieces would be the most interesting to see, and what pieces would actually move during the transformation." Another preparatory step was an elaborate, computer generated animatic. Visual effects supervisor John Knoll employed Electric Image - a 3-D software program - to generate a three-dimensional representation of the spot. "Initially it was just something to show the agency," explained Goldman, "something that would get them comfortable with our approach. John built a rough model of the Formula One and then moved three sections of it; the tail piece, the nose and the wheels. We represented the additional moving elements with pieces of flat art that we shot with a video camera. We put the animatic together at a video bay - combining the twodimensional and three-dimensional elements - and it did a pretty good job of illustrating the transformation. In fact, it turned out to be very helpful when we did it for real." Computer-aided design was also instrumental in making an aesthetic determination regarding the background for the transforming car. "Initially we were going to put the car in a lavish set, but Ketchum didn't want that. They wanted it to look like an underground garage, as opposed to the extremely stylized sets you see in a lot of car commercials now. So we went out and shot real underground garages and scanned that imagery into the computer. Utilizing Adobe Photoshop - which was written by John Knoll and his brother Thomas - we worked with about ten different backgrounds and put the image of the car against each of them to decide which background plate looked best." With testing completed, the effects team determined that the spot would require four separate and impeccably aligned elements: a real Formula One racecar to drive into frame; a quarter-scale Formula One with movable sections; a full-scale Integra cut up into sections; and a real, uncompromised Integra to drive out of frame. We lined up the model and the real car to camera and then matched their motion in Harry." To achieve the transformer-toy-like moves, the quarterscale Formula One was divided into sections and mounted on motion control pylons. "There were three primary actions that the model Formula One performed: its nose turned up, its rear foil collapsed and its wheels turned around. Those were all mechanical pieces controlled by rod mechanisms attached to motion control motors." A full-scale Integra was also cut into pieces and mounted on motion control supports. 'We probably could have built a completely convincing computer model of the car and done the effect digitally," Goldman observed, "but car companies aren't really comfortable with that yet. They don't like the idea of their product being represented by a computer generated image. In some ways, it makes more sense to 106 * CINEFEX 55 use the real thing anyway; the client can provide us with cars that actually exist, and we can cut them up. So the whole transforming effect was done with these three-dimensional pieces; there were no twodimensional objects at all. For example, when the door of the Integra comes up from the bottom, that was a real Acura door that we had cut out of the real car and mounted to a motion control model mover. It was physically moved into position and framesynchronized to the camera." Both the quarter-scale racecar and the cut-up full-scale Acura were shot in two passes: a beauty pass and a frontlight-backlight matte pass. The two elements were next aligned to create the illusion of the Formula One car transforming into the Integra. "The hardest part of the spot was just lining everything up. Since everything had been shot separately, we had to line the elements up looking through the camera - which was really difficult, especially since we had to access the elements in true threedimensional perspective. For example, the rear end of the Integra does this little flip move and, as it does, you see its metallic 'innards.' If we had tried to move the whole rear piece as one element, it would have been too heavy. So we cheated the scale. We cut the piece in half; and as it turns over, you see that it's not really as wide as the width of the car, but then it slides in and fits." Aligning the rotation of the tires from the racecar to the tires of the Integra also presented a challenge due to the differing dimensions of the two vehicles. "The tires were a problem because the wheelbase of the Formula One was longer than the wheel base of the Acura. The tires were also bigger. So when the Formula One wheels turned in, we also had to reposition them in Harry and perform an extended dissolve and some matte work to make that transition smooth. We built mattes for both wheels, and slid them across in the Harry so they would transition into the smaller wheelbase of the Integra." Another particularly tricky aspect of the spot was that the driver in the racecar would be sitting substantially lower than he would in the Integra. "We had to raise the driver up in frame. In the racecar, you could only see his head; but in the Integra, which was higher, you would see his head and shoulder. So after he drove in, we had to move his body from the seat of the racecar up into the seat of the Integra. We shot a separate element of him in order to make that transition. We shot him frontlight-backlight, sitting all by himself, and then moved that element into position in the Harry. Then another element wiped by and we transitioned to the element of him inside the Integra." Once all the separate film elements had been shot, Jonathan Keeton at Western Images put them together on a Quantel Harry. "It was one of those projects that never really looked good until it was completely finished and put together," Goldman noted. 'We showed the agency a version of it when it was ninety-five percent done, but they still couldn't quite imagine how it was going to look when it was all cleaned up and finalized. It was like watching dailies of a movie where a guy is supposedly falling off a mountain, but you can still see the wires attached - it just doesn't have any impact. But when you see him falling without any attachments, it's amazingly effective. It was the same thing with the Integra spot Until all the parts of the transition were really clean and seamless and completely free of any little thing that gave away the gag, it just didn't seem like that great a spot. But when the whole thing looked as if it was happening right before your eyes, then it was really impressive." ACURA PRECISION CRAFTED PERFORMANCE•

EFFECTS SCENE: IN THE DIGITAL DOMAIN article by Don Shay While only a few major firms have dominated the visual effects field in the years since Star Wars and Close Encounters of the Third Kind, challengers have stepped forth from time to time to throw down the technological gauntlet. Some have clawed their way into the pantheon of effects providers, while others have stumbled and fallen by the wayside. Others still have been content to carve off a small piece of the increasingly decentralized effects action now in favor with cost-conscious producers. So why should the formation of Digital Domain warrant more than a wait-and-see reaction in the film community? Certainly not the size of its facility - at the time of its February birth announcement, it had none. Nor the impressive nature of its equipment inventory - only a handful of computer graphics workstations were on line. Nor its kick-off project - none was even mentioned. What immediately established Digital Domain as a contender in the effects field was its trio of highprofile players at the helm. First there was writerdirector-producer James Cameron, whose last three films had won visual effects Oscars and, in the process, opened Hollywood's eyes to the limitless capabilities of computer generated imagery. Next there was creature creator Stan Winston, himself a threetime Oscar winner and one of the preeminent names in makeup and animatronic effects. Then there was Scott Ross, former general manager of Industrial Light & Magic and group vice president of LucasArts' entertainment division. "At the core of Digital Domain," said Ross, "is our belief that there is going to be a digital revolution throughout the world which will be all-pervasive and will change the way we learn, the way we communicate, the way we entertain ourselves. As TV was to the world, this will be - and then some. And it will happen in our lifetime. As a group, we knew that we wanted to play a part in it, but the big question was, 'When is it going to happen and how is it going to happen?' There are no answers to that right now. So how do we position ourselves in an industry that doesn't exist yet? Our experience and expertise is in motion pictures - and the situation right now is that the film industry probably puts more of an investment into digital image-making than any other industry. So our short-term plan is for Digital Domain to be a digital production facility. We believe that will put us in the forefront of new digital technologies." Unlike most effects companies which have been capitalized by specific projects, full funding for Digital Domain comes from a corporate giant - International Business Machines. When Jim and Stan and I got together, we started thinking about the kinds of companies we would like to have as partners," Ross continued. "We felt fairly comfortable that we could raise the money, but we wanted something beyond that. So we put together a list of companies by areas of business - hardware companies, software companies, telecommunications companies, entertainment companies, et cetera - and we took the five top companies in each area and built a matrix on top of that. We asked ourselves: 'Do they get the digital revolution? Is their corporate culture in line with ours? Do they understand creativity? What are their resources and assets?' Interestingly enough, IBM was not on the list. Because of Jim's position in the industry, we were able to speak to people at the very highest levels of these Fortune 100 corporations - and with the exception of one or two, there was interest in every one." A chance call to IBM multimedia executive Kathleen Earley produced an unexpected response. Within forty-eight hours, a team of executives was en route to brief the principals of Digital Domain on plans for a digital production studio that IBM had had on the drawing board for nearly two years. "When we reviewed their documents and heard what they had to say," Ross remarked, "we found almost a mirror image of what our goals and objectives were. To use a baseball analogy, most of the companies we spoke to wanted to play ball. Some of them didn't know how to hold the bat. Others were just stepping into the batter's box. IBM was on third base! They had already done two years of internal research and development." Before long, IBM was an equal partner in Digital Domain, with a commitment to fully fund the company until it reached self-sufficiency - in about eighteen months, as projected. "Every other visual effects facility has been capitalized by projects," observed Ross. "Consequently, their research and development has been stipulated by the particular project on which they are working. So their thinking is often not far-reaching or longterm. It's the production mentality - spit and glue and baling wire to get the job done today so we can put it up on the screen tomorrow. We feel really lucky that we have the capital to be able to be longer-term, more strategic thinkers and planners in developing our assets." Though IBM, with its Power Visualization System, is in stiff competition with Silicon Graphics for a share of the lucrative computer graphics hardware market, its commitment to Digital Domain was nonconditional. In fact, Digital Domain is currently testing numerous animation and rendering packages on a battery of Silicon Graphics workstations arrayed at the Stan Winston Studio while the company's eventual headquarters is being readied in Venice. "Right now," said Ross, "we're invested to the tune of a couple million dollars in SGI platforms. They have some new systems that we haven't driven yet, but the amount of applications already ported to SGI is considerable. Here's a company that has built its business around image generation. On the other hand, IBM, with its PVS, is the fastest gun in town right now; and I've had conversations with the people in research at IBM regarding the future of their systems, and our group is impressed. In terms of platforms, the problem as I see it right now is that the central core rendering systems of these networks have about a twenty-four- to thirty-six-month payback. At the top of the priority list for Digital Domain is to make digital technology more user-friendly and accessible to mainstream film artists. "Our objective is to open up vistas for filmmakers who have been techno-averse and are very anxious about getting involved in new technology. If we can overcome that anxiety and give them something - as opposed to taking something away - that will help open up the digital marketplace. Today there are probably ten or fifteen filmmakers who feel comfortable or have the skill to be able to work in the medium - and the four or five major facilities slice each other up trying to get their business.
