direction is to try to open up that marketplace and get more filmmakers involved in the technology by having them be involved in the process." Though their focus will be on digital technologies, the principals of Digital Domain intend for the facility to be a full-service effects shop - with some exceptions. "If by a full-service company you mean Industrial Light & Magic," said Ross, "that's not what we're going to be. We will not, for example, have a creature shop, for the simple reason that we are associated with what I think is the finest creature shop in the world, Stan Winston Studio. We will not have a model shop. Instead, we will work with people who create high-quality models and subcontract them. Motion control stages? Right now, the state of the art is such that I don't believe in the next two or three years it will be possible to produce, at a reasonable cost, models inside a computer that are photorealistic enough and have the kind of motion and lighting you can get on a motion control stage. So our plan right now is to enter into long-term leases on motion control equipment that we will put on our stages. We're not going to build it; we're not going to own it — because in three years, my crystal ball says we probably won't be doing things that way any112 * CINEFEX 55 more. Where we're going to make our investment is in computer technology." Were Digital Domain to do nothing but projects produced by James Cameron and his Lightstorm Entertainment, it would probably be enough to keep most companies busy. And in fact, among its first assignments will be effects work for the upcoming comedy adventure True Lies, written and directed by Cameron, starring Arnold Schwarzenegger. Also on the docket is another Lightstorm project, Strange Days, written by Cameron and slated for director Kathryn Bigelow. But there are other projects as well. Though the company is constrained from confirming or denying its involvement, it has been reliably reported that Digital Domain is at work on an enormous Terminator 2 multimedia attraction for the Universal Studios tours. Also under discussion is their participation in director Neil Jordan's upcoming Interview with the Vampire. There are a lot of people making incredible promises and talking about visions of the future," Ross cautioned. "We've all heard it before. But a lot of those promises have been empty. And then he puts up walls and makes sure he doesn't step over the abyss." With Scott Ross managing day-to-day operations - and Brooke Breton, an associate producer and effects overseer on the last three Star Trek features, signed on as production chief - just how much of themselves will James Cameron and Stan Winston contribute to Digital Domain? By way of response, Ross reflected on his four-year stint at ILM. "When I was at ILM, everywhere I went people would ask me, What's it like to work with George Lucas?' And I would have to say I have no idea. Over the years I was there, I met him maybe fifteen times, and never once had a one-on-one conversation with him. So it's a really different environment for me to work with Jim Cameron and Stan Winston. Both are very much involved in the company. We have a meeting once a week for updates; and every time I need them to be involved, they are involved - which is important, because to have one filmmaker speak to another is, I think, very powerful. "As I see it, there are five things that this company needs to do in special effects and film. We need to deliver very high-quality images; we need to deliver them on time; we need to deliver them on budget; we need to do it at a reasonable price; and we need to get the creative community involved in the process. When I was at ILM, I was only able to do three out of the five. When I got there, they were already delivering high-quality images. During my tenure, we progressed to the point where we were never late on any of our delivery dates and we never, ever went over budget. And that was really important, because if you look at the landscape at the time, there were a lot of companies missing budgets and blowing release dates. But I could never deliver the work at a reasonable price, and I could not get the creative community involved. With the technology and the capitalization and the creative participants that we have in Digital Domain, I think all five of these objectives are well within reach."

QUICK CUTS: A CRASH IN THE ANDES article by Jody Duncan Based on actual events, Alive is the remarkable story of young rugby players who survived a devastating plane crash in a remote region of the Andes. Trapped at the crash site for more than two months without food, the victims eventually - and reluctantly - turned to cannibalism in order to sustain life. Given the subject matter, it was not surprising when the Frank Marshall film earned an 'R' rating from the Motion Picture Association of America. By some accounts, however, it was not only the issue of cannibalism, sensitively portrayed, that earned the film its restricted rating, but also the harrowing plane crash which opens the film. Realized by Industrial Light & Magic - under visual effects supervisor Scott Farrar - Alive's opening sequence was one of the most riveting and convincing plane crashes ever committed to celluloid. "The most difficult part of the project was to make the crash look realistic, and not fantasy-style," Farrar commented. "We derived as much information as possible from the survivors. We also scouted locations with Frank and director of photography Peter James to determine the sequence of events and how they would unfold and where they might occur in the mountainscapes. Frank knew that the plane crash had to be frightening and very exciting - it had to really grab the audience, because it was the first thing they were going to see in the movie." While engaging ILM as insurance, Marshall and producer Robert Watts intended initially to achieve as many of the opening shots as possible in an air-toair shoot with a real plane. Although optimistic, the filmmakers were well aware of the potential pitfalls. "Both Frank and Robert Watts have a lot of experience with these kinds of things," noted Farrar, "and so they knew that it was entirely possible to shoot a real plane, with a real sky, against real mountains, Industrial Light & Magic modelmakers Tony Sommers and Lore Peterson ready a miniature airliner for a major crash scene in Alive, a true account of survival in the Andes by director Frank Marshall. and still not get the shots they needed. But if it worked, the shots would look great. So they got a real plane and painted it; and they went up and shot for a couple of days." Unfortunately, the shoot proved largely unsuccessful - primarily because the story required very specific conditions for each segment of the crash. "There were important storytelling points to get across," said Farrar. "Basically, the sequence is divided into three stages: stage one, the plane is above the clouds; stage two, the plane descends into the clouds; stage three, the plane finally emerges just in time for the pilot to realize he is heading straight for a mountain. So there was an important weather sequence to follow there, and it just wasn't possible to get it with the air-to-air shots." Taking a small film crew to the location site in the Canadian Rockies, Farrar set about shooting aerial plates that would serve as backgrounds for a number of composite shots employing airplane models. "We had a Wescam, and we spent a week just shooting backgrounds. Each day there was a weather change, and we were always up around ten thousand feet - very high, very scary - going across those mountains. For some of the shots, I wasn't sure in my own mind what the composition would be or what the framing would be, so we just shot a variety of moves from a helicopter." In addition to shooting plates for the twelve shots in which a miniature plane would be used, the crew also filmed some scenes that had been slated for the main unit. "We were having ideal weather up there - ideal in that there were the cloudy conditions called for in the storyboards - so I decided that we should go ahead and shoot those additional plates, just so Frank would have them in his back pocket. As it turned out, some of those shots did wind up being used." The opening sequence begins with the plane in midair. "Frank wanted that first shot to be a nod to George Lucas," Farrar revealed, "with the plane enCINEFEX 55 • 117 FAU FUERZA AEREA URUGUAYA

tering very close to the camera and then flying away slowly - like the beginning of Star Wars." To achieve the effect, the ILM model shop constructed an eight-foot-long replica of the live-action plane. "Bill George was the art director and in charge of the model shop. Together with John Goodman - one of our main model builders - he came up with a method for doing fiberglass casting that produced really great detail on the skin of the airplane. You could see the little rivets and what looked like panels of metal stuck together - it all read on film." The completed model was shot motion control on stage. "Normally we would have used bluescreen, but since this was a very shiny plane - which would have been hard to shoot bluescreen because of reflections - we decided to do a double pass. First we photographed the plane against black; then we photographed the same plane, painted black, against white. A shiny white plane against a whitish sky is the worst possible situation for trying to get a matte: but we decided to go ahead with it, because if it worked out, it would be the best solution. And it worked very well. We also set up a kind of treadmill rig to create reflections on the belly and under the wings of the plane so that it would look like it was 118 * CINEFEX 55 actually flying over the mountains - which is something we could not have done if we were shooting it against bluescreen." As the sequence continues, the plane descends through a thick bank of clouds, emerging to reveal its perilous proximity to the mountain peaks as the pilot attempts to climb to a higher altitude and thus avoid impact. "To shoot these plates, we had to get pretty close to the mountain ridges ourselves. The hardest part was just establishing the scale of those mountains - it was extremely difficult to tell how big or how close they were. So we had to put far more speed into the plate than we had anticipated. Even flying at 120 miles per hour with the helicopter, we had to keep undercranking the camera - going from twenty-four frames per second down to twelve and six and sometimes three frames per second, just to make it look as if the plane was going fast enough." For the flight crew's POV, a full-size cockpit section was shot against bluescreen, and the resulting element was composited with an aerial plate of the fast-approaching mountain peak. "After we'd shot the bluescreen footage, we added shake to each and every element as we put them together in order to create the illusion of the plane shaking violently The breakaway plane was suspended from a tower rig that was later erased from the film via digital image processing. as it struggled to climb upward." A bluescreen setup was also used to achieve shots of passengers falling out of the doomed plane as it begins to break apart in the air. "We had stunt people sitting on airplane seats that were rigged to slide back on a track - as if the seats were being sucked out of the plane - and then tilt down on a hinge to simulate falling. Some of the people were cabled so they could be yanked out of their seats. The whole setup was shot in front of a bluescreen, then matted into the aerial backgrounds." With the pilots unable to divert the disaster, the plane crashes into the mountainside, splitting apart at the midsection and, subsequently, losing its tail and wings. An eight-foot breakaway airplane was employed for the shots. "Both the tail section and the front end of the model were heavily reinforced. The midsection was a nonreinforced area, built out of many layers of plastic and metals and foil and wire, so that when it burst open it would have a layered metal look, like a real airplane would." For the second breakaway shot, in which the plane loses its tail and wings, the model was attached to a steel tower which was propelled down a track at approximately twenty-five miles per hour toward a miniature mountain set erected in the ILM parking lot. "We had the rig aimed at a particular angle so that the plane would be dragged past this big plaster and aluminum foil mountain ridge we had built. Literally, we just preset it so that it would hit correctly, then backed the whole rig up and sent it down the track, photographing it with a camera on a dolly so there was a sense of air-to-air photography." The rig, which was fully visible in the shots, was removed digitally by Stuart Robertson and Dave Carson. "Digital rig removal allowed us to do the shot this way," observed Farrar. "We were able to have a big, solid rig positioned at just the angle we wanted, without having to worry about hiding it in the shot. It was a really wonderful marriage of old and new production techniques." Through both those old and new techniques, ILM provided a heart-stopping opening to Alive - an opening that in all probability could not have been realized in any other way. "Doing a sequence like this is all a matter of controlling the environment and every little aspect of the action," Scott Farrar concluded, "and the only way to really do that is through visual effects."

EFFECTS SCENE: CINEMATIC ARCHAEOLOGY article by Scott MacQueen The year is 2061, and Jurassic Park is a 'lost film. The original camera negative went, along with Universal City, in the San Fernando Quake of'96. The protection interpositive was purchased by the Shaw Brothers in 1998 as stock for Barney No Gyakushu. The YCM protection masters, acquired by the Film Foundation following public outcry over the Barney debacle, vanished in a paper trail tracing them to now-demolished storage vaults outside Muscle Shoals, Alabama. Magnetic disc archive masters - along with all magnetic media in the northern hemisphere - were degaussed by solar flares in 2028. Farfetched? Yes, but not impossible. This is essentially the fate of the original The Lost World, which made as much of an impact in 1925 as Jurassic Park has in 1993. The verisimilitude of Willis O'Brien's animated dinosaurs caused preview critics to wonder if the beasts were real. The boundaries of visual effects were redefined, audiences were awed and the producers' bank accounts swelled. By 1929, The Lost World was withdrawn from release and all 35mm prints and the foreign negative were ordered destroyed, though the domestic negative remained in storage. In 1930, the title was licensed to Kodascope Libraries, a subsidiary of Eastman Kodak created to service the nascent nontheatrical and educational market. At Kodascope, dupe negatives of Hollywood feature films were routinely trimmed by half to a standard five-reel length. Not only would entire subplots and characters vanish, but individual sequences would be reduced to the most basic narrative. Content too strong for the school and church trade was weeded out in the process. With the subsequent loss of the original negative - due to nitrate decay or because silent films were deemed unworthy of prolonged storage by the studio - only the truncated Kodascope version was thought to have escaped extinction. Even surviving Kodascope originals, however - printed on 16mm diacetate safety stock - are quite contrasty and grainy and shrunken with age. In 1990, while producing for Lumivision a laserdisc release of The Lost World - or rather, what was left of it - I began to chart the film's checkered history. The good news was that the motion picture collection at George Eastman House had swooped down in 1949 and grabbed the Kodascope 35mm nitrate dupe negatives just as the failing 16mm division was about to junk them. A complete 16mm master print and, later, 35mm fine-grain masters of three reels were made before the nitrate decomposed. This material allowed our laserdisc version, rendered at a credible frame rate, to look vastly superior to any copy of the film seen since 1925 - but it was still only half the show. Reports that complete versions of The Lost World exist in various private collections have proliferated over the years, but to date have been wholly unsubstantiated. Bits and pieces have turned up, however. Thanks to Jere Guldin, the UCLA Film & Television Archive has preserved the original theatrical trailer - containing two animation cuts among its five 'new' shots. A 365-foot roll of nitrate print exists at the Library of Congress. After the laserdisc release, I had an opportunity to examine that nitrate roll, still in excellent condition. Culled and saved by an old projectionist from an early release print, the scene fragments are elaborately tinted in at least ten hues. There are a dozen 'new' shots, including a traveling matte that combines animation with glass painting and live-action as the brontosaurus ambles past the lecture hall in London. In the fall of 1991, I received a phone call from Pierce Rafferty whose New York film library, Petrified Films, had acquired the Warner Brothers stock shot library. Among the nitrate reels, they had discovered an 800-foot roll of dinosaurs from The Lost World - raw animation takes with slates, mostly from scenes no longer in the film. The footage runs about eight minutes at sound speed. Seeing these outtakes is like peeking over Willis O'Brien's shoulder in the studio. The scenes were deleted, not for content but because they were spoiled takes. The fact that they are unfamiliar shots is lucky coincidence. Imagine the groaning and cursing when these dailies came in and the crew realized that several days' work was ruined because the raw stock had been fogged in loading or an animator was caught at the table for one frame. Their tragedy is our treasure, however, as these flash frames give us a window into the making of The Lost World that has never before been available. Among other things, they disprove the long-held popular belief that, except for the stampede sequence, O'Brien did all of the animation alone - for he is not among the gentlemen caught inadvertently by the lens. Moreover, the production slates identify the sequence animators by name. By far, the most accomplished animation in the surviving version of the film is the battle between the monoclonius and the allosaur. An additional piece of this sequence exists in the outtakes, as a stegosaur - who wound up on the cutting room floor in 1930 - approaches the monoclonius almost playfully. O'Brien's name as animator is chalked on the slate, a firm and fair signature on the sequence. Fluidly wrought, dramatically staged and lit, it is worthy of the best in King Kong. Comparatively, the trachedon sequence is rather amateurish. In fact, it has always been hard to believe that the same man could have executed both sequences, en- . couraging tactless animation afficionados to crack wise about O'Brien's legendary drunkenness. The slates for this sequence reveal the animator as 'Roop.' Almost certainly, this is J.L. Roop, whose jerky manipulation of crudely designed dinosaurs for the Andy Clyde parody The Lost Whirl makes that 1928 Bray Studios short one of the oddest footnotes in the history of dimensional animation. Most sequences are of a pastoral nature, suggesting that O'Brien's primary concern with his creatures was that of a naturalist, not a monster-maker. The dinosaurs eat, preen and tend to their young. Several takes are intact of the mother triceratops sensing danger, then herding her calf to safety before confronting the allosaurus. There is a wonderful new long shot of the lake rimmed by cliffs, with a family of trachedons on the far shore and a clutch of brontosaurs feeding on treetops in the foreground, bickering and thieving the foliage from each other. There is much closeup and medium-shot coverage of creatures and sequences for which only long shots remain in the existing version of the film. Particularly fascinating is the brontosaur, whose nostrils and diaphragm flex as he breathes. With Petrified's enthusiasm and blessing, donations were raised among a concerned group of animation buffs and professionals to pay for an archival CINEFEX 55 • 123

Though barely half of the silent film classic The Lost World survives today, efforts are underway to restore as much of it as possible. Among recent findings is an eight-minute roll of dinosaur outtakes that had been rejected for technical problems of one sort or another. In addition to providing alternate takes for shots that have been lost for more than half a century, these illuminating morsels dispel the popular belief that Willis O'Brien animated all but a few stampede scenes himself, as other animators are specified on some of the shot slates and even, upon occasion, captured inadvertently on film. 124 • CINEFEX 55 dupe negative. Though in excellent physical condition, the nitrate treasure was shrunken slightly, making it impossible to print on a conventional optical printer without register error and probable damage to the original. Sean Coughlin and Tony Munroe of Cinetech, a film restoration lab in Burbank, copied the film carefully on an optical step printer fitted with registration pins specially modified to accept the shrunken film without tearing the perforations. A liquid gate was utilized to prevent imprinting base scratches in the original. The new negative was presented to Chris Horak at Eastman House for safekeeping. Horak had already determined to restore the short version of The Lost World to a new printing negative, filling it out with any new material that could be located. Repeated requests to the Library of Congress to access their roll for preservation and incorporation into the archival negative have been unaccountably ignored. Ironically, the former Soviet bloc has been more cooperative. In late 1992, the Filmovy Arciv in Czechoslovakia reported having a complete nitrate print and agreed to make it available to Lastman House. Initial excitement ran high, but was soon tempered when the find was downsized to five reels with Czech intertitles - only half of the film. But as this is half of the theatrical version, a chance exists to boost the content of the surviving Kodascope version significantly. The outtakes may likewise be a useful resource in the reconstruction, as may the odd shots in the UCLA trailer. A further report suggests that the Cinematheque in Belgium might have several more minutes of unique footage in 16mm. As for the Library of Congress roll, Washington has still not called back. Whether The Lost World will ever be recovered completely is uncertain, but more material has surfaced at this late date than could be reasonably expected. The problem now is largely financial. With the current low funding for archival work and a dearth of fiduciary angels committed to film preservation, this work will probably proceed slowly over several years. Estimates to restore The Lost World run in the neighborhood of $25,000 - about what it costs to digitally composite two elements for the simplest fifteen-second matte shot in a film like Jurassic Park. Many pay lip service to preserving our film heritage, but few show the color of their money for orphaned public domain films, particularly the But the struggle continues. Perhaps one day, all of Professor Challenger's dinosaurs will be rediscovered and returned once more to The Lost World.

LASERDISC REVOLUTION: JURASSIC REALITY column by David C. Fein Since the early days of moviemaking, dinosaurs have been resurrected from extinction by a succession of filmmakers intent upon capturing the imagination of a fascinated public. Beginning with the cartoon simplicity of Gertie the Dinosaur, progressing through the majestic creations of Willis O'Brien and Ray Harryhausen, digressing along the way with overblown iguanas and rubber-suited Godzillas, and expanding breathtakingly into Jurassic Park, each project has relied upon its own particular brand of movie magic to bridge the millennia. Characteristically, the makers of such fare have been concerned more with entertainment value than with accurate depiction of prehistoric animals, either physiologically or behaviorally. But as effects techniques have progressed from cartoon animation to stop-motion animation to animatronic puppetry to computer generated imagery, each prehistoric representation has been greeted by an increasingly informed and sophisticated audience. For this reason, it is incumbent upon the filmmaker and effects provider today to examine carefully the evergrowing body of dinosaur evidence and incorporate the latest scientific revelations into their projects. For the filmmaker intent upon accuracy in dinosaur effects, one of the best compilations of information on the subject is the Arts & Entertainment cable network's 1991 documentary series Dinosaurs!, now available on laserdisc ($69.95) from Lumivision. Comprised of four one-hour episodes hosted by Walter Cronkite, this series and its companion book by David Norman provide a thorough scrutiny of dinosaur behavior - hunting practices, communication, family structure - in addition to a detailed examination of dinosaur anatomy. Each of the four episodes is comprehensive in its study of a clue in the mystery of dinosaur evolution. "The First Clue: Tale of a Tooth," focuses on William Canon Buckland's deduction that a fossilized tooth discovered almost two hundred years ago came from a giant reptile, probably a distant relative of a lizard. His discovery introduced the world to its first dinosaur - megalosaurus - and Buckland reasoned that the shape of the tooth implied that the creature had used its teeth to cut open its prey, causing it to bleed to death, rather than going for a quick kill. His studied examination of megalosaurus and its presumed behavioral characteristics would set the standard for further scientific investigation into the nature of these ancient animals. The opening episode also provides an introduction to the science of paleontology and presents a number of its foremost practitioners. In an unexpected appearance, Ray Harryhausen who brought dinosaurs to life in films ranging from The Animal World to The Valley of Gwangi to One Million Years B.C. - is seen visiting the Natural History Museum in London, where he examines a skull of an ancient predator and ponders the animal's ability to pick up a human being. Harryhausen is later seen with sculptor Robbie Braun who demonstrates an animatronic allosaur named 'Alice' that he is constructing for a museum. Braun explains how he researched the allosaurus in order to accurately design the life-sized reproduction. Alice is reintroduced at the beginning of the next episode as a group of youngsters learn about dinosaurs by observing her programmed behavior. "The Fossil Rush: Tale of a Bone" recounts the discovery of additional dinosaur species during the nineteenth-century 'Dinosaur Rush' spearheaded by Edward Drinker Cope and Othniel Charles Marsh, bitter rivals who devoted themselves to amassing large collections of dinosaur bones, while striving with equal diligence to demean or destroy the other's findings. Featured also in this episode is a glimpse of what is presumed to be the very first dinosaur movie - Gertie the Dinosaur, by Winsor McCay - which featured a cartoon brontosaurus whose antics include tossing an elephant off into the distance and eating a large tree practically whole. Later in the show, an important discovery of dinosaur skin texture imprints is discussed as sculptor Stephen Czerkas works to construct an exact replica of a prehistoric beast. The remainder of the episode examines the dinosaur in art. "Birth of a Legend: Tale of an Egg" covers theories of how nesting practices, communication, colors and sexual attraction may have affected the dinosaurs' lifestyle. Also discussed is current speculation by revisionist paleontologists that dinosaurs - long thought to be cold-blooded - were in fact warm-blooded animals, sparking new theories that dinosaur skin color may have been brighter and more colortul than originally supposed and may well have played a role in attracting mates. The final episode, "Giant Birds of the Air: Tale of a Feather," introduces archaeopteryx, considered the missing link in dinosaur evolution. With both reptilian and birdlike characteristics, archaeopteryx lends credence to current theories that dinosaurs may have evolved into modern-day birds. The controversy over extinction theories is also examined. Was extinction brought on by changing climates, or did a giant meteor strike the earth causing cataclysmic devastation? We may never know for sure. The episode concludes with a suggestion, presented humorously, that man, too, may one day become extinct - displaced perhaps by 'dinosauroid,' an imaginary being based on a half-serious thought experiment by Dr. Dale Russell, who speculated that this fanciful extrapolation might have been the product of dinosaur evolution had dinosaurs survived. Each episode of Dinosaurs! features scientifically accurate visual effects, beginning with superb pencil-sketch animation of a pair of deinonychus feet marching to the beat of the opening music, followed by a pan up to the animal's head just before the opening title. For the rest of the series, the dinosaur 'actors' are rod-puppet models constructed mostly by Peter Minister, with additional ones attributed to Lyons Model Effects. Photographed against bluescreen, the puppets are matted into actual environments. Throughout the series, some of the dinosaur effects have been edited into short sequences that tell a story. For example, the first episode features a megalosaurus attack on an unsuspecting iguanodon. Rapid cross-cutting between predator and prey ends eventually with a touching closeup of the victim's eye closing for the last time. Other dinosaur attacks in the series are less stylized. The effects work, which appears to have been produced entirely on video, is highly entertaining and adds significantly to the narrative. The companion book includes a glimpse into the special effects employed for the series, though the descriptions are very basic. Arts & Entertainment did a more detailed 'making of videotape which is available when the series is purchased through its television offer. CINEFEX 55 • 129
